title: The Divine Liturgy
hook: the Orthodox service, much of it from Chrysostom's time, sung start to finish

segments.voice: Yesterday, first communion, and how churches differ on when a child first comes to the table. Your line was the first taste. Which first bite did you take slowly? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

Smoke from a censer, drifting up past painted faces of saints. Candles everywhere. Hardly any pews; people stand. A choir somewhere you can't quite see, holding one long chord. Then a deacon comes out through a door in the icon screen, carrying a heavy gold-covered book held high. Soon the readings begin, and before them he sings out a short call, loud enough to wake anyone drifting off: Wisdom! Let us attend! Everyone straightens. This is the Divine Liturgy, the Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, and nearly all of it is sung. Today's word: the Divine Liturgy.

First, the name. Liturgy is the church's word for worship offered together. Divine, because Orthodox Christians understand it as heaven's worship, joined for a while on earth. The service used most Sundays carries the name of Saint John Chrysostom, a preacher of the early church. Tradition credits him with shaping it. Second, it's sung. Nearly every line is chanted or sung, by priest, deacon, choir and people, back and forth. The deacon calls out a petition for peace, for the sick, for travelers, and the people answer each one: Lord, have mercy. Again. And again. The answer stays the same while the needs change. Third, the movement. Twice the clergy come out in procession. First with the gospel book, the little entrance. Later with the bread and wine, the great entrance, while the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn, which asks the people to lay aside all earthly cares. Then, as the bread and wine are offered, the people sing a hymn built on the song the prophet Isaiah heard the seraphim singing: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as joining the angels' worship. Fourth, the call. Again and again the deacon says it: let us attend. Wisdom, let us attend. Before the readings, before the creed, before the gifts. It isn't decoration. It's a wake-up call for a mind that wanders, sung over and over, because minds wander over and over.

Here's the practice: listen to a sung liturgy. If you can, find a recording of the Divine Liturgy, or any old church music sung by voices, and let it play quietly. If you can't, just listen to the room around you instead. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow the words. Let the sound come and go. Each time you notice your mind has wandered off, don't scold it. Just say inside, let us attend, and come back to the sound. If you pray, you can join the old answer: Lord, have mercy. The bell holds the time.
The Divine Liturgy. The Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, sung nearly from start to finish, which carries the name of John Chrysostom and comes to the table near its end.
Your line: let us attend. Today, before one conversation that matters, say it inside, let us attend, and then actually listen. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians gather on Sundays for the Divine Liturgy, usually the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, which is chanted or sung throughout; worshipers often stand, light candles, venerate icons and receive communion at the end.

original.note: Greek: let us attend, let us pay attention — the deacon's call before the readings in the Divine Liturgy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long, foreign service you'd sit through.
what it means: worship sung together from start to finish, with processions, incense and a table, where the Orthodox say they stand with the angels.
what a scholar hears: the people sing Isaiah's "holy, holy, holy," so an old temple vision becomes part of a Sunday service, joined with the angels.

notes: Editor: fixed the hook's count ('two words' for a four-word English call) and placement (the gospel-book entrance and 'let us attend' are separate moments; the call now comes before the readings); the liturgy's Sanctus is now 'a hymn built on' Isaiah 6:3, since its wording differs from the KJV; 'from the first word to the last' softened to 'nearly all', as the homily is spoken; 'stand with the angels' reworded; the liturgical call is no longer in quotation marks.

'Wisdom! Let us attend!' and 'Lord, have mercy' are rendered from the liturgy's Greek (Σοφία· Ὀρθοί. Πρόσχωμεν; Κύριε ἐλέησον) in common English wording, not from a specific copyrighted translation; confirm acceptable as quotation marks inside speech or switch to paraphrase.

Chrysostom attribution softened to 'carries the name' and 'tradition credits him with shaping it'; the script drops the index hook's 'much of it from Chrysostom's time' under the claims rule. Confirm.

The hook scene has 'hardly any pews'; some Orthodox parishes, especially in North America, have pews. Confirm the scene reads as one church, not all. 'Nearly every line is chanted or sung' and 'sung from the first word to the last' follow the index; confirm (homily and some announcements are spoken).
The Sanctus is sung during the anaphora; the 'Holy God, Holy Mighty' (Trisagion) is a different hymn, not mentioned. Confirm placement wording 'as the bread and wine are offered'.
The etymology of liturgy (leitourgia, public service) was cut under the claims rule; the script says only that it is the church's word for worship offered together.
Original: Πρόσχωμεν; confirm accent and pronunciation.
Audit (2026-10-02): the word segment said the liturgy 'ends at the table'; it ends with a dismissal after communion, so now 'comes to the table near its end'. Isaiah 6:3 checked exact.
